newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe PC makers fret at Intel chip debut.
newsitem.headline: Europe PC makers fret at Intel chip debut.

text.p: Intel Corp on Wednesday said its new multimedia computer chips should ensure it remains one of the world's most profitable companies, but European computer makers set to use the chips had less to rave about.

Intel's MMX technology produces the kind of TV-like images that make both teenage joystick jockeys and professional videographers crave new PCs, but European vendors fear weak continental economies will bring a slowdown in growth in 1997.

"It will be a tough year in the consumer sector in Germany," Compaq Computer GmbH salesman Karl Tucholski said over the stereophonic surround-sound emanating from one of his firm's Presario MMX systems at Intel's launch in Munich.

Market researcher IDC forecasts European PC sales will grow 8.5 percent this year, after rising 12 percent to 16.5 million PCs in 1996 and jumping 35 percent in 1995. IDC also forecasts 1998 growth of only six percent -- the slowest in 10 years.

"Consumer confidence is not there for people to go out and spend money on a new computer," said IDC's Simon Pearce in London. "And we're starting to get worried that a lower estimate might have to be brought forward to 1997."

With France and Germany struggling under double-digit unemployment rates, and other countries straining finances to qualify for European monetary union, growth in home PC sales will be limited over the next two years, Pearce said.

At the same time, IDC expected growth in corporate buying to ease because many companies have just finished upgrading old 486 machines to Pentium chips and Microsoft Corp.'s Windows 95 operating system.
"We're not looking for the next upgrade cycle to really kick in until late 1998," Pearce said.
Most of the PC makers ready to ship MMX PCs are aiming them at buyers backed by corporate budgets.

The MMX PCs shown in Munich included a dozen desktop systems priced from 3,300 marks ($2,100) to 7,000 marks -- well above the 2,000 mark price point that most buyers are willing to pay. A Toshiba Europe GmbH portable that uses the MMX capabilities for mobile videoconferencing was listed at 13,500 marks.

"People who don't have PCs now aren't the ones who are going to buy MMX systems," said Heiner Bruns, a Dell Computer GmbH salesman. "It will be experienced users and corporate users. We don't expect a wave of new customers."

Intel is more optimistic, saying MMX PCs will make it easier for users to set up their machines to understand voice, transmit phone calls and pictures over the Internet and play three-dimensional games.
"We expect clear growth in Europe," said spokesman Heiner Genzken. "Growth in the core European countries is not so healthy but there are emerging markets in the south of Europe."

Since the MMX chips are priced only about 10 percent more than standard Pentiums -- $550 for a 200 megaherz MMX versus $509 for a standard version, for example -- buyers who want Pentium PCs should be able to afford the extra cost for MMX capabilities, Genzken said.

Analysts expected Intel's MMX chips to make a bigger splash right away in the United States, where many home buyers held off holiday purchases in anticipation of the new technology and the economic outlook is positive.

Demand for PCs and Intel chips is also stronger in the U.S. because of favourable pricing. PCs are about 30 percent more expensive in Europe because of value-added taxes and higher business costs, Pearce said. ($1=1.5711 Mark)
